title: Sum of All Odd Length Subarrays
summary: Add up the sums of every contiguous subarray of arr whose length is odd.
statement:
You are given an array of positive integers `arr`. Consider every contiguous subarray of `arr` whose length is odd (1, 3, 5, …). Return the sum of all the elements of all those subarrays.

Follow-up: can you do it in O(n) time and O(1) space?
hints: With n ≤ 100, adding up every odd-length subarray directly works, especially with prefix sums. For O(n), think about one element at a time instead of one subarray at a time.
Index i is in (i + 1) × (n − i) subarrays: i + 1 possible starts times n − i possible ends.
A subarray [l, r] has odd length exactly when l and r have the same parity. Of the (i + 1)(n − i) subarrays containing i, ⌈(i + 1)(n − i) / 2⌉ have odd length. Add arr[i] times that.
explain: The odd-length subarrays of `[1,4,2,5,3]` are the five single elements (sum 15), the three of length 3: `[1,4,2]` = 7, `[4,2,5]` = 11, `[2,5,3]` = 10, and the whole array (15). 15 + 7 + 11 + 10 + 15 = `58`.

title: Number of Zero-Filled Subarrays
summary: Count the contiguous subarrays of nums in which every element is 0.
statement: Given an integer array `nums`, return how many contiguous, non-empty subarrays consist only of zeros.
hints: A block of z consecutive zeros contains z × (z + 1) / 2 all-zero subarrays. Can you avoid computing blocks separately?
Count each subarray at its right end. If the current run of zeros (ending at i) has length run, how many all-zero subarrays end exactly at i?
Keep run = run + 1 on a zero and 0 otherwise, and add run to the answer at every index. Use a 64-bit total.
explain: `[1,3,0,0,2,0,0,4]` has two blocks of two zeros. Each block holds `[0]` twice and `[0,0]` once: 3 subarrays. Two blocks give `6`.

title: Vowels of All Substrings
summary: Add up, over every substring of word, the number of vowels (a, e, i, o, u) it contains.
statement:
Given a string `word`, return the total number of vowels (`'a'`, `'e'`, `'i'`, `'o'`, `'u'`) in every substring of `word`, added up.

A substring is a contiguous, non-empty run of characters. The answer can be larger than a 32-bit integer.
constraints: word consists of lowercase English letters
hints: There are about n² / 2 substrings, too many to list for n = 10⁵. Flip it: how many substrings contain the character at index i?
A substring containing index i starts at one of 0 … i and ends at one of i … n − 1.
Every vowel at index i contributes (i + 1) × (n − i). Compute it in 64-bit arithmetic.
explain: The substrings of "aba" are "a", "b", "a", "ab", "ba" and "aba", with 1, 0, 1, 1, 1 and 2 vowels. The total is `6`.

title: Total Hamming Distance
summary: The Hamming distance of two integers is the number of bit positions where they differ. Return the sum of the Hamming distances over every pair of numbers in nums.
statement:
The Hamming distance between two integers is the number of bit positions where their bits differ.

Given an integer array `nums`, return the sum of the Hamming distances between all pairs of numbers in `nums` (each unordered pair once).
constraints: The answer fits in a 32-bit integer
hints: Comparing every pair is O(n²), up to 5 × 10⁷ pairs. Bits are independent, though: look at one bit position at a time.
At bit b, suppose ones numbers have a 1 and zeros have a 0. Which pairs differ at bit b?
Exactly the ones × zeros mixed pairs. Add ones × (n − ones) over all 32 bit positions: O(32 · n).
explain: In 4 bits: 4 = 0100, 14 = 1110, 2 = 0010. 4 and 14 differ in 2 positions, 4 and 2 in 2, and 14 and 2 in 2, so the total is `6`.

title: Bitwise XOR of All Pairings
summary: Form nums3 from nums1[i] ^ nums2[j] for every pair (i, j). Return the XOR of all the values in nums3.
statement:
You are given two arrays `nums1` and `nums2` of non-negative integers. Imagine an array `nums3` that holds `nums1[i] ^ nums2[j]` for every pair of indices `(i, j)`, each pair exactly once.

Return the bitwise XOR of all the integers in `nums3`.
hints: nums3 can have 10¹⁰ elements, so don't build it. XOR is commutative and associative, so you only need to know how many times each original value ends up in the big XOR.
Each nums1[i] is paired with every element of nums2, so it appears nums2.length times. Each nums2[j] appears nums1.length times.
x ^ x = 0, so a value appearing an even number of times cancels. XOR all of nums1 if nums2.length is odd, and all of nums2 if nums1.length is odd.
explain: nums3 = [8,0,7,2, 11,3,4,1, 9,1,6,3] (2, 1 and 3 each XOR-ed with 10, 2, 5 and 0). XOR-ing all twelve gives `13`, the same as XOR-ing 2, 1 and 3 (each appears 4 times, an even number, so they cancel) with 10, 2, 5 and 0 (each appears 3 times).

title: Sum of Absolute Differences in a Sorted Array
summary: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order. For each i, compute the sum of |nums[i] − nums[j]| over all j, and return these sums as an array.
statement:
You are given an integer array `nums` sorted in non-decreasing order.

Return an array `result` of the same length where `result[i]` is the sum of `|nums[i] − nums[j]|` over all indices `j` (including `j = i`, which adds 0).
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: Computing each result[i] with its own loop is O(n²). Use the fact that the array is sorted.
Every element before i is ≤ nums[i] and every element after is ≥ nums[i], so the absolute values can be dropped: the left part is nums[i] × i − (sum of the first i elements).
With prefix sums p, result[i] = (nums[i] · i − p[i]) + ((p[n] − p[i + 1]) − nums[i] · (n − 1 − i)).

title: Sum of Distances
summary: For each index i, add up |i − j| over every other index j with nums[j] == nums[i] (0 if there is none). Return these sums.
statement:
You are given a 0-indexed integer array `nums`. Build an array `arr` of the same length where `arr[i]` is the sum of `|i − j|` over every index `j ≠ i` with `nums[j] == nums[i]`. If no such `j` exists, `arr[i]` is 0.

Return `arr`.
hints: Only indices holding the same value interact. Group the indices by value (they come out sorted if you collect them left to right).
Inside one group the problem is "sum of absolute differences in a sorted array" applied to the indices.
For the k-th index j of a group: (j · k − sum of the indices before it) + (sum of the indices after it − j · (size − 1 − k)). Track the running sum and use 64-bit values.
explain: The value 1 sits at indices 0, 2 and 3. For index 0 that is |0−2| + |0−3| = 5, for index 2 it is 2 + 1 = 3, for index 3 it is 3 + 1 = 4. The 3 and the 2 appear once, so they get 0: `[5,0,3,4,0]`.

title: Subarray Product Less Than K
summary: nums holds positive integers. Count the contiguous subarrays whose product is strictly less than k.
statement: Given an array of positive integers `nums` and an integer `k`, return the number of contiguous subarrays whose product of all elements is strictly less than `k`.
hints: The values are positive, so extending a subarray never lowers its product, and shrinking it never raises it.
For each right end r, find the leftmost l such that the product of nums[l..r] is < k with a sliding window. Every start from l to r then works.
Add r − l + 1 for each r. If k ≤ 1, no product of positive integers is < k: return 0 (and avoid an endless shrink loop).
explain: The 8 subarrays with product below 100 are [10], [5], [2], [6], [10,5], [5,2], [2,6] and [5,2,6]. [10,5,2] has product exactly 100, which is not strictly less, so the answer is `8`.

title: Count Subarrays Where Max Element Appears at Least K Times
summary: Let m be the largest value in nums. Count the contiguous subarrays in which m appears at least k times.
statement:
You are given an integer array `nums` and a positive integer `k`. Let `m` be the maximum element of the whole array.

Return the number of contiguous subarrays in which `m` appears at least `k` times.
hints: "At least k" is monotone: if [l, r] has k copies of m, so does every [l′, r] with l′ ≤ l.
Slide a window and, for each r, move l forward while the window still has at least k copies of m. Afterwards [l, r] has fewer than k copies, but [l − 1, r] had k.
So every start 0 … l − 1 works for this r: add l. The total can exceed 32 bits.
explain: The maximum is 3. The subarrays containing at least two 3s are [1,3,2,3], [1,3,2,3,3], [3,2,3], [3,2,3,3], [2,3,3] and [3,3]: `6`.

title: Sum of Subarray Ranges
summary: The range of a subarray is its largest element minus its smallest. Return the sum of the ranges of every contiguous subarray of nums.
statement:
The range of a subarray is the difference between its largest and smallest elements.

Given an integer array `nums`, return the sum of the ranges of all its contiguous, non-empty subarrays.

Follow-up: can you do it in O(n) time?
hints: With n ≤ 1000, fixing the start and extending the end while tracking the running min and max is O(n²) and fast enough.
For O(n), split it: the answer is (sum of every subarray's maximum) − (sum of every subarray's minimum).
Each sum is a contribution problem: a[i] is the minimum of (i − prev smaller) × (next smaller-or-equal − i) subarrays, found with a monotonic stack. Do the same for maximums.
explain: The subarrays of [1,2,3] are [1], [2], [3] (range 0 each), [1,2] and [2,3] (range 1 each) and [1,2,3] (range 2). The total is 0 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 1 + 2 = `4`.

title: Minimum Fuel Cost to Report to the Capital
summary: n cities form a tree (roads) and city 0 is the capital. Each city sends one representative to the capital; every city has a car with `seats` seats, and representatives may switch cars or share them. Each road travelled by one car costs one litre. Return the minimum total fuel.

perf.label: a path of 100,000 cities
perf.gen: int[][] a0 = new int[99999][]; for (int i = 1; i < 100000; i++) a0[i - 1] = new int[] { i - 1, i }; int a1 = 1;

statement:
A country has `n` cities numbered `0` to `n − 1`, connected by `n − 1` bidirectional roads that form a tree (`roads[i] = [a, b]`). City `0` is the capital.

Every city except the capital sends one representative to the capital. Each city has a car with `seats` seats. A representative may ride in their own car or get into another one at any city they pass through. Driving a car along one road costs one litre of fuel.

Return the minimum number of litres needed for all representatives to reach the capital.
constraints: roads forms a tree on 0 … n − 1
hints: Look at one road at a time. Which representatives must cross the road between a city v and its parent (towards the capital)?
Exactly the people in v's subtree, and they can all meet at v first and share cars. So that road costs ⌈size(v) / seats⌉ litres, no matter what happens elsewhere.
One traversal from the capital computes every subtree size; add ⌈size / seats⌉ for every non-capital city. Use an iterative traversal: a path of 10⁵ cities overflows recursion.
explain: Cities 1, 2 and 3 are each one road from the capital. Each representative drives straight there in their own car, one litre each, for `3`. Sharing wouldn't help: they don't pass through each other's cities.

title: Sum of Subsequence Widths
summary: The width of a sequence is its maximum minus its minimum. Return the sum of the widths of all non-empty subsequences of nums, modulo 10⁹ + 7.
statement:
The width of a sequence is the difference between its maximum and minimum elements.

Given an integer array `nums`, return the sum of the widths of all its non-empty subsequences. A subsequence keeps the original order but may skip elements; different index choices count as different subsequences. Return the answer modulo `10⁹ + 7`.
hints: There are 2ⁿ − 1 subsequences, far too many. The width only depends on which values are picked, not their order, so you may sort.
After sorting, nums[i] is the maximum of the subsequences that pick it plus any subset of the i smaller elements: 2^i of them. It is the minimum of 2^(n − 1 − i).
Add nums[i] × (2^i − 2^(n−1−i)) modulo 10⁹ + 7, with precomputed powers of two. Fix a negative running total at the end.
explain: The non-empty subsequences of [2,1,3] are [2], [1], [3], [2,1], [2,3], [1,3] and [2,1,3], with widths 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 2 and 2. Their sum is `6`.

title: Total Appeal of A String
summary: The appeal of a string is the number of distinct characters in it. Return the total appeal of all substrings of s.
statement:
The appeal of a string is the number of distinct characters it contains. For example, the appeal of `"abbca"` is 3 (`'a'`, `'b'` and `'c'`).

Given a string `s`, return the sum of the appeals of all its substrings.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: A letter that appears several times in a substring adds only 1 to its appeal. Decide which copy gets the credit: the first one in the substring.
s[i] is the first copy of its letter in substring [l, r] exactly when l is after the previous occurrence of that letter (call it last).
So s[i] adds (i − last) × (n − i). Keep last[26] (−1 when unseen) and use a 64-bit total.
explain: "abbca" has 15 substrings. Adding their numbers of distinct letters (5 of length 1 with appeal 1, then "ab" 2, "bb" 1, "bc" 2, "ca" 2, "abb" 2, "bbc" 2, "bca" 3, "abbc" 3, "bbca" 3 and "abbca" 3) gives `28`.

title: Count Unique Characters of All Substrings of a Given String
summary: For a string t, countUniqueChars(t) is the number of characters that appear exactly once in t. Return the sum of countUniqueChars over every substring of s (substrings at different positions count separately).
statement:
For a string `t`, let `countUniqueChars(t)` be the number of characters that appear exactly once in `t`. For example, `countUniqueChars("LEETCODE") = 5` (`L`, `T`, `C`, `O` and `D`).

Given a string `s`, return the sum of `countUniqueChars(t)` over every substring `t` of `s`. Substrings at different positions are counted separately, even if they are equal. The answer fits in a 32-bit integer.
constraints: s consists of uppercase English letters
hints: Flip it: for each index i, in how many substrings is s[i] the only copy of its letter?
The substring must start after the previous occurrence of s[i] and end before the next occurrence.
With prev[i] (−1 if none) and next[i] (n if none), s[i] adds (i − prev[i]) × (next[i] − i).
explain: The substrings of "ABC" are "A", "B", "C", "AB", "BC" and "ABC". Every letter in each of them appears once, so they add 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = `10`.

title: Count Subarrays With Score Less Than K
summary: The score of an array is its sum multiplied by its length. nums holds positive integers; count the non-empty contiguous subarrays whose score is strictly less than k.
statement:
The score of an array is the sum of its elements multiplied by its length. For example, the score of `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]` is `15 × 5 = 75`.

Given an array of positive integers `nums` and an integer `k`, return the number of non-empty contiguous subarrays whose score is strictly less than `k`.
hints: All values are positive, so shrinking a subarray lowers both its sum and its length: if [l, r] is valid, so is every [l′, r] with l′ ≥ l.
Slide a window: add nums[r], then drop from the left while sum × (r − l + 1) ≥ k.
Then every subarray ending at r and starting in [l, r] is valid: add r − l + 1. Use 64-bit arithmetic for the sum, the score and the count.
explain: The subarrays with score below 10 are [2] (2), [1] (1), [4] (4), [3] (3), [5] (5) and [2,1] ((2 + 1) × 2 = 6). [1,4] already scores 10, so the answer is `6`.

title: Sum of Total Strength of Wizards
summary: For a contiguous group of wizards, its total strength is (the weakest strength in the group) × (the sum of all strengths in the group). Return the sum of the total strengths of every contiguous group, modulo 10⁹ + 7.
statement:
`strength[i]` is the strength of the i-th wizard in a line. For any contiguous group of wizards, its total strength is (the strength of its weakest wizard) × (the sum of all strengths in the group).

Return the sum of the total strengths of all contiguous groups, modulo `10⁹ + 7`.
hints: Credit each group to its weakest wizard (break ties consistently). A monotonic stack gives, for each i, the range of starts and ends where strength[i] is the minimum.
For those groups you need the sum of their sums. With prefix sums P, a group [l, r] sums to P[r + 1] − P[l]: each P[r + 1] appears once per possible start and each P[l] once per possible end.
Runs of consecutive P values are ranges of a second prefix sum PP over P. Combine (starts) × (sum of P over the ends) − (ends) × (sum of P over the starts), all modulo 10⁹ + 7.

title: Sum of Distances in Tree
summary: An undirected tree has n nodes labelled 0 … n − 1 and the given edges. For every node i, return the sum of the distances (number of edges) from i to all other nodes.
statement:
There is an undirected tree with `n` nodes labelled `0` to `n − 1` and `n − 1` edges given in `edges`.

Return an array `answer` of length `n` where `answer[i]` is the sum of the distances between node `i` and every other node. The distance between two nodes is the number of edges on the path between them.
constraints: edges forms a tree on 0 … n − 1
hints: A BFS from every node is O(n²), too slow for 3 × 10⁴. First get answer[0] cheaply: each node below an edge uses that edge once on its way to 0, so answer[0] is the sum of all subtree sizes (except the root's).
Now move the root from a parent p to its child c. The size[c] nodes in c's subtree each get one step closer; the other n − size[c] nodes each get one step farther.
So answer[c] = answer[p] − size[c] + (n − size[c]). Two traversals, O(n); make them iterative to stay safe on long paths.
explain: Node 0 is 1 edge from 1 and 2, and 2 edges from 3, 4 and 5: 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8. Node 2 is 1 from 0, 3, 4 and 5 and 2 from 1: 6. Doing the same for every node gives `[8,12,6,10,10,10]`.
